Abstract: Over the past decades, advances in the diagnosis and treatment of congenital heart disease have reshaped its epidemiology. Congenital heart disease is now increasingly a chronic, lifelong disorder, with adult survivors outnumbering affected children in many countries. This demographic transition has shifted the focus from preventing early mortality towards optimizing long-term health and managing comorbidities. Authors: Doug Doucette

Source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: This paper examines what coarse-grained transport graphs, such as Ulam matrices, can and cannot prove about escape in measure-preserving dynamical systems. It separates two questions: whether chaos remains confined and whether it actually escapes. The central result is an asymmetry. Upper bounds on escape transfer reliably from the matrix to the map. item.title: Maintaining cognitive gains in type 2 diabetes: Barriers, supports, and patterns of strategy use
item.description:
Authors: Heather E. Cuevas, Jeeyeon Kim, Shenell Wood

Source: PLoS ONE

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution

Abstract: In this study, we report how adults with type 2 diabetes maintained cognitive strategies learned in the Memory, Attention, and Problem-Solving Skills for Diabetes (MAPSS-DM) intervention. We identify three patterns of strategy maintenance that emerged from follow-up interviews with 19 participants: sustained use, partial use, and discontinuation. Factors that supported long-term use of strategies include consistent routines, social support, and personal value placed on cognitive improvements. Barriers include inconsistent routines, lack of support, and negative emotions such as guilt. This study emphasizes the need for personalized, adaptable cognitive interventions and ongoing support to promote lasting benefits in both cognitive function and diabetes self-care.

Abstract: Is there a positive counterpart to negligence? Across two studies, we found that people consistently judged agents whose unwitting actions or omissions were beneficial to be praiseworthy.
